questions.statement: What is the passive voice of this sentence?
questions.context: A sentence reads: 'The new library was built in 2019.'

options.text: The builders built the new library in 2019.
options.feedback: In the active, the builders become the subject and perform the action that the passive attributes to the library.

options.text: The new library was building in 2019.
options.feedback: 'Was building' is a passive progressive, which is not the simple event described in the sentence.

options.text: The new library is built in 2019.
options.feedback: 'Is built' would place the construction in the present, while the original names the year 2019.

options.text: The new library built in 2019.
options.feedback: A passive sentence needs an auxiliary before the participle, and none appears here.

questions.explanation:
The passive moves the object of the active sentence into the subject position and adds an auxiliary. Recovering the active form is the fastest way to check whether a candidate transformation is correct.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the active equivalent?
questions.context: A sentence reads: 'Rice is grown by thousands of small farmers in this region.'

options.text: Thousands of small farmers grow rice in this region.
options.feedback: Moving 'rice' back to the object position and naming the farmers as the subject produces the active form.

options.text: Thousands of small farmers are growing rice here.
options.feedback: 'Are growing' is the active of the present continuous, which is not the tense of the original sentence.

options.text: Rice grows by thousands of small farmers in this region.
options.feedback: 'Rice' cannot be the subject that grows the crop, so this reading is nonsensical.

options.text: Thousands of small farmers grew rice in this region.
options.feedback: 'Grew' is the past simple and changes the time reference of the sentence.

questions.explanation:
An active equivalent must contain exactly the same participants, tense and meaning as the passive. Checking all three prevents students from producing a sentence that is active but says something different.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence explains why the report uses the passive voice?
questions.context: A report reads: 'Fifty hectares of forest were destroyed by the fire last year.'

options.text: The action matters more than who performed it
options.feedback: Reports often keep the affected party as the subject and omit the agent, so the focus stays on the forest.

options.text: The writer wants to name the person who started the fire
options.feedback: If the agent were the point of the sentence, the active form would be the appropriate choice.

options.text: The sentence must be shorter in the active form
options.feedback: The passive is not used for length, and here the active sentence would be no shorter than the passive.

options.text: The active form would be grammatically impossible
options.feedback: An active form exists and is perfectly grammatical, as the equivalent question demonstrates.

questions.explanation:
Writers choose the passive when the agent is unknown, unimportant or already mentioned. Learning to ask why a text uses the passive is part of critical reading, because the choice of voice shapes what the reader notices.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which active sentence does the passive describe?
questions.context: A sentence reads: 'The road is being repaired at the moment.'

options.text: Someone is repairing the road at the moment.
options.feedback: 'Is being' plus participle is the passive continuous and its active counterpart uses 'is repairing' with an agent.

options.text: The road repairs itself at the moment.
options.feedback: A road cannot repair itself, so the passive subject cannot be the agent of the action.

options.text: The road repaired at the moment.
options.feedback: 'Repaired' would be the simple past, which the continuous form excludes.

options.text: Someone repaired the road at the moment.
options.feedback: The present continuous indicates an action in progress, not a completed one.

questions.explanation:
The passive continuous describes an action in progress at the moment of speaking. Its active equivalent always requires an agent, since the true subject of a repair is a person or a crew.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What construction does this sentence use?
questions.context: A sentence reads: 'He had his car serviced before the trip.'

options.text: The causative with 'have' plus object plus past participle
options.feedback: 'Have' plus object plus participle describes having something done by someone else, which is the causative use.

options.text: The passive voice with 'had' as the past auxiliary
options.feedback: 'Had' can be the auxiliary of the past perfect, but here it belongs to the causative construction.

options.text: The present perfect with a participle
options.feedback: The present perfect would need 'has' plus participle with the subject performing the action.

options.text: A relative clause modifying 'car'
options.feedback: No relative pronoun appears, so the sentence contains no relative clause.

questions.explanation:
The causative has two forms: 'have' plus object plus participle for arranged services, and 'get' plus object plus participle for arrangements the speaker obtains. The subject arranges the work rather than doing it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the active equivalent?
questions.context: A sentence reads: 'The letters have been delivered.'

options.text: The postman has delivered the letters.
options.feedback: The present perfect passive becomes the present perfect active with the agent as subject and the object after the verb.

options.text: The letters has delivered the postman.
options.feedback: Agreement is wrong: a plural subject 'letters' requires 'have', not 'has'.

options.text: The letters have delivered themselves.
options.feedback: Letters cannot deliver themselves, so the passive subject cannot become the agent here.

options.text: The postman has been delivered the letters.
options.feedback: The structure mixes the auxiliary of a passive with the word order of an active and is ungrammatical.

questions.explanation:
The transformation of the present perfect passive follows the same pattern as any other passive: auxiliary plus participle becomes have plus past participle with the agent promoted to subject. The tense is preserved throughout.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option explains the structure of this sentence?
questions.context: A sentence reads: 'It is widely believed that the species is disappearing.'

options.text: An impersonal passive report with a that-clause as subject
options.feedback: 'It' is a dummy subject, 'is believed' is the passive, and the that-clause carries the real content of the report.

options.text: A passive sentence in which 'the species' is the agent
options.feedback: 'The species' sits inside the that-clause as its subject and is the object of the verb 'believe', not the agent.

options.text: A causative construction with 'it' as the object
options.feedback: No causative construction is present, since there is no object receiving an arranged action.

options.text: A question in passive form
options.feedback: The sentence is a declarative statement and contains no auxiliary of question formation.

questions.explanation:
Reporting verbs such as 'believe', 'say' and 'report' are often used in the impersonal passive, which lets a writer avoid naming a source. This structure is extremely frequent in journalistic and academic English.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the causative correctly?
questions.context: A contractor is discussing a building project.

options.text: They had the roof repaired before the rains began.
options.feedback: In the causative, the object sits between 'had' and the past participle, which is the fixed pattern of the construction.

options.text: They had repaired the roof before the rains began.
options.feedback: 'Had repaired' is a past perfect active form in which the contractor does the work personally.

options.text: They repaired the roof had before the rains began.
options.feedback: The participle cannot follow the object in this construction, so the word order is wrong.

options.text: They had the roof repair before the rains began.
options.feedback: The participle must be in the past form 'repaired', not the base form 'repair'.

questions.explanation:
The causative's fixed order is have plus object plus past participle. Students who place the participle immediately after 'have' produce a past perfect instead, which changes who performs the action.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the sentence tell us about the speaker?
questions.context: A speaker says: 'I had my hair cut before the ceremony.'

options.text: The speaker arranged for a hairdresser to cut the hair
options.feedback: The causative always implies that someone else performs the action the speaker arranged.

options.text: The speaker cut her own hair at home
options.feedback: Cutting one's own hair would require the active form 'I cut my hair'.

options.text: The speaker's hair was already cut when she arrived
options.feedback: The past participle and the causative structure indicate an arrangement completed before the ceremony, not a pre-existing condition.

options.text: The speaker will cut her hair after the ceremony
options.feedback: The sentence is entirely in the past, so no future action is being described.

questions.explanation:
The causative separates the person who arranges an action from the person who performs it. That distinction is the whole point of the construction and it is often tested directly in exams.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What time relation does this sentence express?
questions.context: A text reads: 'The bridge had been damaged before the earthquake struck.'

options.text: The damage was already present before the earthquake began
options.feedback: The past perfect places the damage earlier than the past event named in the second clause.

options.text: The earthquake damaged the bridge during the quake
options.feedback: A simultaneous event would use the past simple in both halves.

options.text: The bridge will be repaired after the earthquake
options.feedback: Nothing in the sentence refers to a future repair.

options.text: The earthquake and the damage happened at the same moment
options.feedback: 'Before' establishes that the two events are not simultaneous.

questions.explanation:
The past perfect always signals that one past event precedes another. It is frequently used with the passive in reports, where the writer establishes what was already known before the incident being described.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this passive construction emphasise?
questions.context: A text reads: 'The proposal was met with strong opposition.'

options.text: The opposition itself rather than the group that expressed it
options.feedback: 'Met with' makes the opposition the subject, so the response is what the sentence presents as important.

options.text: The identity of the members of the committee
options.feedback: The group is not named at all in this sentence, so its identity is not the point.

options.text: The date when the opposition was expressed
options.feedback: No date appears anywhere in the sentence.

options.text: The reason why the committee objected
options.feedback: The sentence states that opposition was strong without giving any reason for it.

questions.explanation:
Several verbs change meaning in the passive, and 'meet' is the standard example in exam material. 'Was met with' always means a reaction was received, never that a meeting took place.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement about this sentence is accurate?
questions.context: A worker says: 'I am having my kitchen redesigned.'

options.text: The worker arranged the work and a designer carries it out
options.feedback: The present form of the causative shows an arrangement in progress, with the designer as the real agent.

options.text: The worker is redesigning the kitchen alone
options.feedback: Doing the work alone would require the active form 'I am redesigning the kitchen'.

options.text: The kitchen is being redesigned by the worker now
options.feedback: That reading would need the passive form 'The kitchen is being redesigned by me'.

options.text: The design has already been completed
options.feedback: Nothing in the present form indicates that the work has already been finished.

questions.explanation:
Causatives exist in the present, the past and the past perfect, and the tense of the auxiliary shows the time of the arrangement itself. This item checks that the student separates the time of arranging from the time of doing.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence has the same modal meaning?
questions.context: A text reads: 'The samples must be tested before the results can be published.'

options.text: The laboratory must test the samples before the results can be published.
options.feedback: A modal passive becomes a modal active with the agent as subject and the modal unchanged before the base form of the verb.

options.text: The laboratory must be testing the samples before the results can be published.
options.feedback: 'Must be testing' is a modal passive continuous, which expresses a different, ongoing obligation.

options.text: The samples must testing the laboratory before the results can be published.
options.feedback: A modal cannot be followed by a gerund with the object in front of it, so the word order is impossible.

options.text: The samples must tested before the results can be published.
options.feedback: A modal never takes a past participle directly, so 'must tested' is ungrammatical.

questions.explanation:
Modals pass unchanged from the passive to the active, which makes this transformation a reliable exercise. The base form after the modal is the feature students most often get wrong.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the passive allow the writer to avoid naming?
questions.context: A text reads: 'Children should be given time to read before being asked to answer.'

options.text: The person who gives the children the reading time
options.feedback: The agent of 'give' is left out, so the sentence focuses on what the children receive rather than on who provides it.

options.text: The children who are reading
options.feedback: The children are named as the subject of the sentence, so they are not what is avoided.

options.text: The time given for reading
options.feedback: The reading time appears in the sentence as the thing given.

options.text: The questions asked afterwards
options.feedback: The questions appear explicitly as the later activity.

questions.explanation:
Advice about children is often written with an agentless passive because the advisor does not want to name a parent or a teacher. The result is a general statement that applies to any adult who supervises reading.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which tense does the passive use in this sentence?
questions.context: A sentence reads: 'The new law has been widely welcomed by farmers in the region.'

options.text: Present perfect passive
options.feedback: 'Has been' plus participle is the present perfect passive, which connects a past event to its current relevance.

options.text: Past simple passive
options.feedback: The past simple passive would use 'was welcomed', and no past auxiliary appears here.

options.text: Present continuous passive
options.feedback: A continuous passive would need 'is being welcomed', which is absent.

options.text: Past continuous passive
options.feedback: The past continuous would require a specific past moment of the action, which the sentence does not name.

questions.explanation:
Tense in the passive is carried entirely by the auxiliary, because the participle never changes. Reading the auxiliary is therefore the fastest way to identify the tense of any passive sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does the writer use two different passives in this report?
questions.context: A news article states: 'Three suspects were arrested in connection with the robbery, and they have since been released without charge.'

options.text: The first records a past event and the second reports a change up to the present
options.feedback: 'Were arrested' fixes a completed action in the past, while 'have since been released' links the outcome to the present moment.

options.text: The first hides the police and the second hides the suspects
options.feedback: Naming an agent is a choice about focus, and the difference between the two clauses lies in tense rather than agent.

options.text: The two passives repeat the same information in two registers
options.feedback: The two clauses report different facts, so they are not a repetition of the same information.

options.text: The second passive is a causative form of the first
options.feedback: A causative would require 'have' plus object plus participle, and no such structure appears.

questions.explanation:
Reporters move from past to present as a story develops, and the passive makes both halves precise without naming an agent each time. Recognising the shift in tense is what lets a reader follow the sequence of events.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option correctly identifies the two tenses present in the sentence?
questions.context: A sentence reads: 'The road was being widened when the accident happened.'

options.text: Past continuous passive and past simple
options.feedback: 'Was being widened' describes work in progress during a past period, and 'happened' is the completed past simple event.

options.text: Past simple passive and past continuous
options.feedback: The order is reversed: the continuous clause comes first and the simple clause second.

options.text: Present perfect passive and past simple
options.feedback: No present perfect auxiliary appears in the sentence, and 'have since' is not present.

options.text: Past perfect passive and present simple
options.feedback: A past perfect would require 'had been widened', which is not the form used.

questions.explanation:
Two tenses can appear in one sentence, and the past continuous passive plus past simple is a frequent combination in news narrative. Each clause is described separately, which is how a student should analyse any long sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the active equivalent of the causative?
questions.context: A homeowner says: 'We are having the fence painted next week.'

options.text: We are arranging for someone to paint the fence next week.
options.feedback: A causative describes an arrangement, and the active paraphrase must make the arrangement and the agent both explicit.

options.text: We are painting the fence next week.
options.feedback: Painting personally would remove the distinction that the causative creates between arranging and performing.

options.text: The fence is painting itself next week.
options.feedback: A fence cannot paint itself, so the fence cannot become the agent of the action.

options.text: We are being painted the fence next week.
options.feedback: The structure misplaces the passive auxiliary and is not a grammatical English clause.

questions.explanation:
The distinction between arranging and performing is the meaning of the causative. Any paraphrase that loses that distinction, such as a plain active, is not equivalent to the original.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence applies the instruction correctly?
questions.context: A writer is told to avoid the passive voice in an essay.

options.text: The research team collected the data over two months.
options.feedback: The agent is named as the subject and the verb follows it directly, which is the active structure the instruction requires.

options.text: The data was collected over two months.
options.feedback: This is the passive form that the instruction explicitly rejects.

options.text: It was collected that the data took two months.
options.feedback: The dummy subject 'it' with an embedded clause is indirect and impersonal rather than active.

options.text: There was collected the data over two months.
options.feedback: An existential 'there' cannot serve as the subject of a transitive passive, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

questions.explanation:
Avoiding the passive in an essay means naming the agent in the subject position. The three distractors represent the passive, an impersonal structure and an ungrammatical attempt, so the exercise tests the transformation itself.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the construction 'was made to' express?
questions.context: A legal sentence reads: 'The witness was made to repeat the statement three times.'

options.text: Someone obliged the witness to repeat the statement against her will
options.feedback: 'Make' plus object plus 'to' plus infinitive is causative and always carries the pressure of compulsion on the object.

options.text: The witness was asked politely and agreed willingly
options.feedback: Politeness and willingness would require a verb such as 'asked', not 'made'.

options.text: The witness repeated the statement on her own initiative
options.feedback: Doing it on her own initiative would need the active form with the witness as subject.

options.text: The witness was instructed to repeat it, without coercion
options.feedback: Coercion is precisely what the causative verb 'make' expresses, so the fourth reading removes its meaning.

questions.explanation: This item separates the causative from the passive, which look almost identical here. In the passive someone did something to the witness; in the causative someone obliged the witness to act, and the second reading is the one that matters legally.
questions.subject: ingles
